account: After the M7.8 earthquake in Türkiye on 6 February 2023, the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) activated, led by the Turkish community Yer Çizenler. It ran Tasking Manager projects for roads and buildings in Türkiye and Syria. HOT's own activation and size-up pages (Internet Archive captures of 7 February and 29 May 2023) mention no AI tool and list no partner requests. Tasking Manager records for the 11 Türkiye projects, which Yer Çizenler ran on HOT's platform, show that the projects were set up with MapWithAI suggestions in the Rapid editor, which Meta maintains. The OpenStreetMap (OSM) wiki page for the response is community-authored and was last modified 5 June 2026. It states that, because of the large project areas, AI-assisted mapping with the RapiD editor was originally encouraged. It proved counter-productive and was then disabled. Research from the University of Colorado Boulder and Indiana University, shared with HOT in August 2023, compared 1,650 Tasking Manager contributors before and during the response. The wiki's only citation for this study is a HOT meeting recording of 9 August 2023. Contributors using RapiD mapped tasks up to 12.4% slower than those not using AI-assisted mapping. Validators reported many data-quality issues from RapiD contributors, which led to RapiD being disabled on all activation projects. The archived settings of all 11 Türkiye projects still list Rapid as an editor. The same wiki page records that OSM data supported rescue coordination by the AKUT Search and Rescue Association and AFAD. It also supported public-health programming in the Kahramanmaraş tent city and the World Bank's GRADE damage report. No cited source documents Microsoft building footprints or HOT's fAIr here, nor any AI role in HOT's 2022 Pakistan floods activation. No cited source covers Cyclone Idai.

fields.account: After the M7.8 earthquake in Türkiye on 6 February 2023, the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) activated, led by the Turkish community Yer Çizenler. It ran Tasking Manager projects for roads and buildings in Türkiye and Syria. HOT's own activation and size-up pages (Internet Archive captures of 7 February and 29 May 2023) mention no AI tool and list no partner requests. Tasking Manager records for the 11 Türkiye projects, which Yer Çizenler ran on HOT's platform, show that the projects were set up with MapWithAI suggestions in the Rapid editor, which Meta maintains. The OpenStreetMap (OSM) wiki page for the response is community-authored and was last modified 5 June 2026. It states that, because of the large project areas, AI-assisted mapping with the RapiD editor was originally encouraged. It proved counter-productive and was then disabled. Research from the University of Colorado Boulder and Indiana University, shared with HOT in August 2023, compared 1,650 Tasking Manager contributors before and during the response. The wiki's only citation for this study is a HOT meeting recording of 9 August 2023. Contributors using RapiD mapped tasks up to 12.4% slower than those not using AI-assisted mapping. Validators reported many data-quality issues from RapiD contributors, which led to RapiD being disabled on all activation projects. The archived settings of all 11 Türkiye projects still list Rapid as an editor. The same wiki page records that OSM data supported rescue coordination by the AKUT Search and Rescue Association and AFAD. It also supported public-health programming in the Kahramanmaraş tent city and the World Bank's GRADE damage report. No cited source documents Microsoft building footprints or HOT's fAIr here, nor any AI role in HOT's 2022 Pakistan floods activation. No cited source covers Cyclone Idai.

purpose: AI-assisted mapping was encouraged to speed building and road mapping over large areas for responders. The OpenStreetMap wiki reports that it slowed mapping and lowered quality in this activation. The claimed benefit was not delivered.
